title: NTA UGC NET English Full Mock Test #07
subtitle: 100 Questions · 200 Marks · Post-2018 NTA Pattern · Zero Answer Bias (25 A/B/C/D) · Reading Comprehension (Q91-100)

items.title: Mock #07 · Q1
items.stem: The epitaph on her tombstone that Emily Dickinson composed herself reads
items.explanation: Emily Dickinson's gravestone in Amherst, Massachusetts, bears the epitaph "Called Back", drawn from the title of Hugh Conway's 1883 novella and forming the entire text of the final letter she wrote to her cousins before her death in May 1886.

items.title: Mock #07 · Q2
items.stem: Women in Love is a sequel to which one of the following novels by D.H. Lawrence?
items.explanation: D.H. Lawrence's novel Women in Love (1920) is the direct sequel to The Rainbow (1915), continuing the emotional, intellectual, and psychological lives of the Brangwen sisters, Ursula and Gudrun.

items.title: Mock #07 · Q3
items.stem:
The following statements relate to the early history of the English language. Identify the set that gives INCORRECT statements :
1. English has borrowed words such as sky, give, law, and leg from Norse.
2. English has also borrowed some pronouns like they, their, them from Norse.
3. In grammar, Modern English is much more highly inflected than Old English.
4. After the Norman Conquest, French became the language of the court, the language of nobility and polite society, and literature.
5. Following the Norman Conquest, French virtually replaced English as the language of the people.
6. Among the French words that came into English are : study, logic, grammar, noun, etc.
items.explanation: Statements 3 and 5 are false: Old English was a synthetic, highly inflected language whereas Modern English is analytic with very few inflections (making 3 false); and after the Norman Conquest, English remained the spoken language of the vast majority of the common people while Anglo-Norman French was confined to the ruling elite (making 5 false).

items.title: Mock #07 · Q4
items.stem:
In which of the texts, the following lines occur?
“Of all the causes which conspire to blind
Man’s erring judgement, and misguide the mind,
What the weak head with strongest bias rules,
Is pride, the never failing vice of fools.”
items.explanation: These lines appear in Part II (lines 201–204) of Alexander Pope's An Essay on Criticism (1711), where Pope warns that intellectual vanity and pride are the primary causes that mislead critics and blind their literary judgment.

items.title: Mock #07 · Q5
items.stem:
Arrange the following in the chronological order of their year of publication:
A. “The Tyger”
B. “The Solitary Reaper”
C. “Adonais”
D. “The Rime of the Ancient Mariner”
E. “Ode to Autumn”
items.explanation: The publication dates of these Romantic poems in chronological order are: William Blake's "The Tyger" (Songs of Experience, 1794), S. T. Coleridge's "The Rime of the Ancient Mariner" (Lyrical Ballads, 1798), William Wordsworth's "The Solitary Reaper" (Poems, in Two Volumes, 1807), John Keats's "To Autumn" (1820), and P. B. Shelley's elegy "Adonais" (1821). This corresponds to A -> D -> B -> E -> C.

items.title: Mock #07 · Q6
items.stem:
The Birth of Tragedy from the Spirit of Music by Friedrich Nietzsche-
A. Examines the origins and development of poetry, specifically Greek tragedy.
B. Argues that Socratic rationalism and optimism led to the death of Greek tragedy.
C. Examines the origin of music and dance in ancient Greece.
D. Argues that Greek tragedy arose out of the fusion of Apollonian and Dionysian elements.
E. Argues that the music is the spirit of tragedy.
items.explanation: In The Birth of Tragedy from the Spirit of Music (1872), Friedrich Nietzsche examines Greek tragic drama (A), argues that tragedy arose from the dialectical balance of Apollonian and Dionysian forces (D), and contends that Euripidean doubt and Socratic rationalism caused its decline (B).

items.title: Mock #07 · Q7
items.stem: …………… attempted to draw a distinction between two kinds of Truth, a theological Truth ‘drawn from the word and oracles of God’ and determined by faith, and a ‘scientific’ Truth based on the light of nature and the dictates of reason.
options: Treatise on the laws of Ecclesiastical Piety
Literature and Pulpit in Medieval England
items.explanation: In Book II of The Advancement of Learning (1605), Francis Bacon drew a fundamental distinction between theological truth drawn from divine revelation and accepted on faith, and scientific truth derived through empirical observation of nature and human reason.

items.title: Mock #07 · Q8
items.stem: Here is a list of early English plays imitating Greek and Latin plays. Pick the odd one out
items.explanation: Christopher Marlowe's Tamburlaine the Great (c. 1587) is a romantic Elizabethan blank-verse tragedy that defies classical unities and models. By contrast, Gorboduc (1561) imitated Senecan tragedy, while Ralph Roister Doister and Gammer Gurton's Needle imitated Roman comedies by Plautus and Terence.

items.title: Mock #07 · Q9
items.stem:
Identify the two previous titles of the poem ‘Out of the Cradle Endlessly Rocking’ as Walt Whitman continued to revise it until it reached the present form in the ‘Sea-Drift’ section of the 1881 edition.

A. ‘Vigil Strange I Kept on the Field One Night’
B. ‘Crossing Brooklyn Ferry’
C. ‘A Child's Reminiscence’
D. ‘The Wound-Dresser’
E. ‘A Word Out of the Sea’

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Walt Whitman first published the poem in the New York Saturday Press in December 1859 under the title 'A Child's Reminiscence' (C); in the 1860 edition of Leaves of Grass it was titled 'A Word Out of the Sea' (E), before being given its definitive title in 1871.

items.title: Mock #07 · Q10
items.stem: Which of the following statements is true in terms of distribution of metrical feet?
options: Anapaestic is to Dactylic as Trochaic is to Iambic
Iambic is to Trochaic as Anapaestic is to Dactylic
Trochaic is to Anapaestic as Dactylic is to Iambic
Dactylic is to Trochaic as Iambic is to Anapaestic
items.explanation: The iamb (u /) is the reverse of the trochee (/ u), and the anapaest (u u /) is the reverse of the dactyl (/ u u).

items.title: Mock #07 · Q11
items.stem:
Match the Term with the Theorist :
(Term) (Theorist)
(a) Negritude  (i) Alice Walker
(b) Womanism  (ii) Jürgen Habermas
(c) Interpellation  (iii) Aimé Cesaire
(d) Public Sphere  (iv) Louis Althusser
items.explanation: Negritude is Aimé Césaire's, womanism Alice Walker's, interpellation Althusser's, and the public sphere Habermas's.

items.title: Mock #07 · Q12
items.stem: Why is "Universal grammar" so called ?
options: It is a set of basic grammatical principles universally followed and easily recognized by people
It is a set of basic grammatical principles assumed to be fundamental to all natural languages
It is a set of advanced grammatical principles assumed to be fundamental to all natural languages
It is a set of universally respected practices that have come, in time, to be known as "grammar
items.explanation: Associated with Noam Chomsky's generative linguistics, Universal Grammar (UG) is so called because it posits an innate set of fundamental grammatical principles and structural constraints shared by all natural human languages.

items.title: Mock #07 · Q13
items.stem:
Which among the following assumptions are not true in the context of diasporic identities?

'A. Migrancy constructs modes of existence and ways of seeing that go beyond actual journey between countries

B. Migrancy can expose the migrants and their children to displacement and fragmentation

C. The dominant narratives of belonging and identity can accommodate those who live in-between

D. Living in-between can be a pleasurable experience

E. Home is a problematic concept

Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below
items.explanation: Statements C and D are false: dominant national narratives of identity typically fail to accommodate individuals living 'in-between,' and diasporic liminality involves dislocation, alienation, and cultural anxiety rather than unproblematic pleasure. In contrast, diaspora theory affirms that migrancy creates new modes of seeing (A), causes fragmentation (B), and complicates the concept of 'home' (E).

items.title: Mock #07 · Q14
items.stem: The 'Vulgate Bible' was prepared to make the Bible available to
items.explanation: Commissioned by Pope Damasus I in AD 382 and translated primarily by St. Jerome into everyday vernacular Latin (editio vulgata, 'common edition'), the Vulgate Bible was prepared to make the Scriptures accessible to the common Latin-speaking people.

items.title: Mock #07 · Q15
items.stem:
Arrange the following works of literature chronologically based on their year of publication:
A. The English Patient
B. The Swinging Bridge
C. Lives of Girls and Women
D. Family Matters
E. Birnam Wood
items.explanation: The chronological order of these works by publication year is: Alice Munro's Lives of Girls and Women (1971), Michael Ondaatje's The English Patient (1992), Rohinton Mistry's Family Matters (2002), Ramabai Espinet's The Swinging Bridge (2003), and Eleanor Catton's Birnam Wood (2023). This corresponds to C -> A -> D -> B -> E.

items.title: Mock #07 · Q16
items.stem:
Jeremy Collier's Short View of the
Immorality and Profaneness of the
English Stage (1698) attacked ______
options: the practice of mixing tragic and comic themes in Shakespeare's plays
the bawdiness of "low" characters in Shakespeare's plays
irreligious themes and irreverent attitudes in the plays of the seventeenth century
the coarseness and ugliness of Restoration Theatre
items.explanation: Jeremy Collier's polemical tract A Short View of the Immorality, and Profaneness of the English Stage (1698) fiercely attacked the sexual coarseness, bawdiness, profanity, and anti-clerical satire of late seventeenth-century Restoration theatre (targeting playwrights such as Congreve, Vanbrugh, Wycherley, and Dryden).

items.title: Mock #07 · Q17
items.stem: Which of the following statements best describes T. S. Eliot's assertion that Shakespeare's Hamlet is an 'artistic failure'?
options: Hamlet's obsession should have been within representational limits
Hamlet's feelings far outweigh the release of his emotions
Hamlet's emotion is not adequately objectified
Hamlet's indecisiveness slows the steady progress of action
items.explanation: In 'Hamlet and His Problems' Eliot says there is no 'objective correlative' for Hamlet's emotion, so it exceeds the facts presented.

items.title: Mock #07 · Q18
items.stem: Which of these lines is NOT in Pope’s Essay on Criticism?
options: “Fools rush in where angels fear to tread”
“A little learning is a dangerous thing”
“Wretches hang that jury men may dine”
“The sound must seem an echo to the sense”
items.explanation: The satirical couplet "And wretches hang that jury-men may dine" appears in Canto III (line 22) of Alexander Pope's mock-epic The Rape of the Lock (1714), whereas the other three famous maxims are from An Essay on Criticism (1711).

items.title: Mock #07 · Q19
items.stem:
Which two of the following events are described in Samuels Pepys's Diary?
A. The Plague in London

B. The Great Fire of London

C. The War of Spanish Succession

D, Essex Rebellion

Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: Kept in shorthand from 1660 to 1669, Samuel Pepys's Diary provides vivid first-hand eyewitness accounts of Restoration London, most famously the Great Plague of London (1665) and the Great Fire of London (September 1666). The Essex Rebellion occurred earlier in 1601, and the War of the Spanish Succession took place later from 1701 to 1714.

items.title: Mock #07 · Q20
items.stem:
"You do not dwell in me nor I in you

however much I pander to your name"

These lines from Geoffrey Hill's "Lachrimae" address
items.explanation: These opening lines are from 'Lachrimae Verae,' the first sonnet in Geoffrey Hill's seven-sonnet sequence 'Lachrimae, or Seven tears figured in seven passionate Pavans' (collected in Tenebrae, 1978), which meditates on religious martyrdom and addresses the crucified Christ.

items.title: Mock #07 · Q21
items.stem:
Match the following :
(Phrases from Poems) — (Titles of Poems)
I. "Sound of stick upon the floor" — 1. "Byzantium"
II. "Hade's bobbin bound in mummy cloth" — 2. "Sailing to Byzantium"
III. "With beauty like a tightened bow" — 3. "Coole and Ballylee, 1931"
IV. "A tattered coat upon a stick" — 4. "No Second Troy"
The right combination according to the code is :
Code : I II III IV
items.explanation: In W.B. Yeats's poetry: 'Sound of a stick upon the floor' appears in 'Coole Park and Ballylee, 1931' (I-3); 'Hades' bobbin bound in mummy-cloth' in 'Byzantium' (II-1); 'With beauty like a tightened bow' in 'No Second Troy' (III-4); and 'A tattered coat upon a stick' in 'Sailing to Byzantium' (IV-2).

items.title: Mock #07 · Q22
items.stem:
Which romantic poet coined the
famous phrase 'spots of time' ?
items.explanation: William Wordsworth coined the phrase 'spots of time' in his autobiographical poem The Prelude (Book XI of the 1805 text; Book XII of the 1850 text) to describe vivid, formative childhood memories that retain a 'renovating virtue' to nourish the mind in later life.

items.title: Mock #07 · Q23
items.stem:
Which among the following is true about Religio Laici?
A. John Dryden wrote Religio Laici.
B. Religio Laici strongly criticized the Anglican Church.
C. Religio Laici means 'A Layman's Faith'.
D. Religio Laici was published in 1690.
E. Religio Laici was a philosophico-religious prose treatise.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: John Dryden wrote Religio Laici (A), which translates to 'A Layman's Faith' (C). Published in 1682 (not 1690), it is a philosophical-religious poem in heroic couplets (not a prose treatise) that defends the Anglican Church's via media against Deism, Catholicism, and Puritanism.

items.title: Mock #07 · Q24
items.stem:
"Fourth World Literature" refers to

I.
the works of native people
living in a land that has been
taken over by non-natives.

II.
the works of black people in
the United States.

III.
the
literature
of
the
marginalized.

IV.
refers to the works of non-
heterosexuals

Of the above
options: I, III and IV are correct
items.explanation: Coined from George Manuel's concept of the 'Fourth World' (1974), Fourth World Literature refers to the writings of indigenous, aboriginal, First Nations, and marginalized peoples whose lands or cultures have been colonized or subordinated within modern nation-states (I and III).

items.title: Mock #07 · Q25
items.stem:
Arrange chronologically the following texts in terms of their years of first publication:
 A. Edmund Spenser's The Faerie Queene
 B. Coleridge and Wordsworth's Lyrical Ballads
 C. Pablo Neruda's Canto General
 D. Charles Baudelaire's The Flowers of Evil
 Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: The chronological order of first publication is Edmund Spenser's The Faerie Queene (1590, A), Wordsworth and Coleridge's Lyrical Ballads (1798, B), Charles Baudelaire's The Flowers of Evil (1857, D), and Pablo Neruda's Canto General (1950, C).

items.title: Mock #07 · Q26
items.stem: Which of the following is another term to describe "art for art's sake" ?
items.explanation: Aestheticism was the late nineteenth-century European arts movement—championed in England by Walter Pater and Oscar Wilde—centred on the doctrine of 'art for art's sake' (l'art pour l'art), which held that art should pursue beauty rather than moral or didactic purposes.

items.title: Mock #07 · Q27
items.meta: Unit IX: Literary Theory post World War II
items.stem:
Assertion (A) :
The orld does not become raceless or ill not become unracialized by
assertion. The act of enforcing racelessness in literary discourse is itself a
racial act.
Reason (R) :
Pouring rhetorical acid on the fingers of a black hand ay indeed destroy
the prints, but not the hand. Besides, hat happens, in that violent, self-
serving act of erasure, to the hands, the fingers, the fingerprints of the one
ho does the pouring ? Do they remain acid-free ? The literature itself
suggests otherwise.
In the context of the statements above,
options: (A) akes complete sense in the light of (R).
items.explanation: In Playing in the Dark: Whiteness and the Literary Imagination (1992), Toni Morrison argues that enforcing racelessness in American literary study is itself an aggressive act of racial erasure; Assertion (A) is fully substantiated by Reason (R)'s caustic metaphor of pouring rhetorical acid.

items.title: Mock #07 · Q28
items.stem: Mr. Pumblechook is a character in:
items.explanation: Mr. Pumblechook is Pip's pompous uncle in Dickens's Great Expectations.

items.title: Mock #07 · Q29
items.stem:
Who among the following believed that rhyme is not an integral part of poetry?
A. William Wordsworth

B. Horace

C. Samuel Daniel

D. Philip Sidney

Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below
items.explanation: Classical Roman poet Horace (in Ars Poetica, written in unrhymed hexameters) and Renaissance critic Sir Philip Sidney (who stated in An Apology for Poetry that 'it is not rhyming and versing that maketh a poet') both maintained that rhyme is merely an ornament rather than the defining essence of poetry. By contrast, Samuel Daniel defended rhyme in A Defence of Ryme (1603).

items.title: Mock #07 · Q30
items.stem:
In a remarkably proleptic insight, a critic wrote the following, anticipating Benedict Anderson’s
definition of the nation as “an imagined political community” :
“Most novels are in some sense knowable communities.  It is part of a traditional method –
an ,underlying ,stance ,and ,approach ,– ,that ,a ,novelist ,offers ,to ,show ,people ,and ,their
relationships in essentially knowable and communicable ways”.
Name the critic and the reference :
options: Van Wyck Brooks, The writer in America
T.S. Eliot, Notes Towards a Definition of culture
Joseph Wood Krutch, The Modern Temper
Raymond Williams, The country and the city
items.explanation: In The Country and the City (1973), Raymond Williams examined how communities and national affinities are imaginatively constructed and perceived across historical transformations of rural and urban spaces, anticipating Benedict Anderson's concept of 'imagined communities'.

items.title: Mock #07 · Q31
items.stem:
Match List - I with List - II.
List - I | List - II
(A) Afro-American Literature | (I) Basudev Sunani
(B) Caribbean literature | (II) Sally Morgan
(C) Australian Aboriginal literature | (III) V. S. Naipaul
(D) Dalit Literature | (IV) Zora Neale Hurston
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The literary traditions match their representative writers as follows: Afro-American Literature with Zora Neale Hurston (A-IV), Caribbean Literature with V. S. Naipaul (B-III), Australian Aboriginal Literature with Sally Morgan (C-II), and Dalit Literature with Odia poet Basudev Sunani (D-I).

items.title: Mock #07 · Q32
items.stem:
Who among the following African novelists was a student of philosophy and literature in
India ?
items.explanation: Somali novelist Nuruddin Farah (born 1945), author of From a Crooked Rib (1970) and Maps (1986), studied philosophy, literature, and sociology at Panjab University in Chandigarh, India, from 1966 to 1970.

items.title: Mock #07 · Q33
items.stem:
According to Ferdinand de Saussure, language is:
A. an interlocking structure.
B. a system of constant change.
C. a system of signs.
D. a self-standing formation.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In Course in General Linguistics (1916), Ferdinand de Saussure defines language (langue) synchronically as an interlocking relational structure (A) and a formal system of signs (C) wherein value is determined by differential relations.

items.title: Mock #07 · Q34
items.stem: The famous text The Empire Writes Back came out in the year:
items.explanation: The Empire Writes Back: Theory and Practice in Post-Colonial Literatures, a landmark foundational text by Australian scholars Bill Ashcroft, Gareth Griffiths, and Helen Tiffin, was published in 1989 by Routledge.

items.title: Mock #07 · Q35
items.stem:
Choose the correct sequence of the following works of Pablo Neruda in chronological order:-
A. Spain in the Heart
B. Works and Book of Twilights
C. The Inhabitant and His Hope
D. Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair
E. The Trying of Infinite Man
items.explanation: The chronological order of Pablo Neruda's early works is: Crepusculario (Book of Twilights, 1923), Veinte poemas de amor y una canción desesperada (Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair, 1924), Tentativa del hombre infinito (The Trying of Infinite Man, 1926), El habitante y su esperanza (The Inhabitant and His Hope, 1926), and his Spanish Civil War volume España en el corazón (Spain in the Heart, 1937). This sequence corresponds to B -> D -> E -> C -> A.

items.title: Mock #07 · Q36
items.stem:
Identify the untrue statement on the
CONTACT ZONE below
options: The contact zone" is a space where disparate cultures meet, clash and grapple with each other
Postcolonial societies "contact" suggests the historical moment when settler and indigenous cultures first met
It is believed that the Contact Zone was largely instrumental in spearheading nationalist movements across the world
The idea of the Contact Zone was first proposed and defined by Mary Louise Pratt's Imperial Eyes : Travel Writing and Transculturation
items.explanation: Coined by Mary Louise Pratt in her 1991 essay 'Arts of the Contact Zone' and her book Imperial Eyes: Travel Writing and Transculturation (1992), the 'contact zone' refers to colonial spaces where disparate cultures meet, clash, and grapple with each other in asymmetrical power relations—not a force for 'spearheading nationalist movements across the world'.

items.title: Mock #07 · Q37
items.stem:
Given below are two statements : One is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R.
Assertion (A): In 19th century, Charlotte Perkins Gilman asserted economic independence over voting rights.
Reason (R): The representation of women as power-seekers was not socially acceptable in 19th century America.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
items.explanation: In Women and Economics (1898), Charlotte Perkins Gilman emphasized women's economic independence as even more foundational than suffrage, while nineteenth-century American gender ideology stigmatized women who sought political power.

items.title: Mock #07 · Q38
items.stem: Under whose presidency was PEN (an international association of poets, playwrights, editors, essayists and novelists) founded by Mrs. Dawson-Scott in 1921?
items.explanation: PEN International was founded in London in October 1921 by English writer Catherine Amy Dawson Scott, with novelist and playwright John Galsworthy serving as its first worldwide president.

items.title: Mock #07 · Q39
items.meta: Unit V: Language: Basic Concepts, Theories and Pedagogy
items.stem:
The term ‘negritude’, coined by Aime Cesaire, was appreciated as well as criticized by critics and thinkers. Select the correct responses that this term received.
A. Senegal Senghor considered this term to be derogatory.
B. Leon Damas didn’t participate in the negritude movement.
C. Creole writers attacked this term for its monolithic look.
D. Nobel Laureate Wole Soyinka considered ‘negritude’ as an unhealthy fetishism of the ‘native’ state.
E. Frantz Fanon was extremely critical of the term “negritude’ and never used it.
items.explanation: Creole theorists such as Jean Bernabé, Patrick Chamoiseau, and Raphaël Confiant critiqued Négritude for postulating a totalizing, monolithic Black identity (C), while Wole Soyinka famously criticized Négritude as a defensive and narcissistic fetishization of racial identity (D). Senghor and Damas were co-founders rather than opponents of the movement, and Fanon actively engaged with Négritude.

items.title: Mock #07 · Q40
items.stem:

items.explanation: In his Preface to Shakespeare (1765), Samuel Johnson defends Shakespeare against neoclassical critics by arguing that Shakespeare preserved the essential Unity of Action (II) while showing that the unities of time and place rest on false assumptions about dramatic illusion (IV).

items.title: Mock #07 · Q42
items.stem:
Who, among the following English
playwrights,
scripted
the
film
Shakespeare in Love ?
items.explanation: British playwright Tom Stoppard co-wrote the Academy Award-winning screenplay for the 1998 film Shakespeare in Love alongside Marc Norman, playfully imagining a love affair that inspires Shakespeare to write Romeo and Juliet.

items.title: Mock #07 · Q43
items.stem:
Examples of poetic compounding are found in the work of which two modernist writers?
(a) Graham Greene
(b) James Joyce
(c) Gerard Manley Hopkins
(d) Stephen Spender
Choose the correct option:
items.explanation: Bold lexical and poetic compounding is a hallmark of both Gerard Manley Hopkins (c, who coined compounds like 'dapple-dawn-drawn' and 'wanwood leafmeal') and James Joyce (b, whose modernist prose in Ulysses and Finnegans Wake abounds in compound neologisms).

items.title: Mock #07 · Q44
items.stem: Identify the title of A.D. Hope's first published book of poems
items.explanation: Australian poet and critic A. D. Hope's first solo published collection of poetry was The Wandering Islands (1955), which established his reputation for neoclassical formal mastery, satire, and eroticism.

items.title: Mock #07 · Q45
items.stem: Which of the following set of characters in Charles Dickens' novels is in the right chronological order?
options: Mr. Bounderby — David Copperfield — Mrs. Mann — Nathaniel Winkle
Nathaniel Winkle — Mrs. Mann — David Copperfield — Mr. Bounderby
David Copperfield — Mr. Bounderby — Nathaniel Winkle — Mrs. Mann
Mrs. Mann — David Copperfield — Nathaniel Winkle — Mr. Bounderby
items.explanation: The correct chronological sequence across Charles Dickens's novels is: Nathaniel Winkle in The Pickwick Papers (1836–1837), Mrs. Mann in Oliver Twist (1837–1839), David Copperfield in David Copperfield (1849–1850), and Josiah Bounderby in Hard Times (1854).

items.title: Mock #07 · Q46
items.stem: What is the content of the suitcases that Lucky carries in the second Act of Waiting for Godot?
items.explanation: In Act 2, Lucky still carries the bag, which Pozzo says holds sand.

items.title: Mock #07 · Q47
items.stem:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R
Assertion A: The best-known cycles of miracle or mystery plays come from York, Wakefield, and Chester.
Reason R: King Alfred encouraged the use of the vernacular in the late ninth century, but he made it clear that this was very much second best, necessitated by the deplorably low standards of Latin learning in his kingdom.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
A is correct but R is not correct
Both A and R are correct but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is not correct but R is correct
items.explanation: Both statements are historically accurate facts from Ronald Carter and John McRae's The Routledge History of Literature in English: the late medieval mystery play cycles came from York, Wakefield, and Chester, while King Alfred promoted Old English vernacular prose in the late ninth century, though R does not explain A.

items.stem:
Read the following passage and answer the questions (46 to 50):

We need to begin by casting doubt on the legitimacy of the notion of literature. The mere fact that the word exists, or that an academic institution has been built around it, does not mean that the thing itself is self-evident.
Reasons—perfectly empirical ones, to begin with—are not hard to find. The full history of the word literature and its equivalents in all languages and all eras has yet to be written, but even a perfunctory look at the question makes it clear that the term has not been around for ever. In the European languages, the word literature in its current sense is quite recent: it dates back—just barely—to the nineteenth century. Might we be dealing with a historical phenomenon rather than an "eternal" one? Moreover, many languages (many African languages, for example) have no generic term covering all literary productions. To these initial observations we may add the fragmentation characteristic of literature today. Who dares specify what is literature and what is not, given the irreducible variety of the writing that tends to be attached to it, from vastly different perspectives?
The argument is not conclusive: a notion may legitimately exist even if there is no specific term in the lexicon for it. But we have been led to cast the first shadow of doubt over the "naturalness" of literature. A theoretical examination of the problem proves no more reassuring. Where do we come by the conviction that there is indeed such a thing as literature? From experience. We study "literary" works in school, then in college; we find the "literary" type of book in specialized stores; we are in the habit of referring to "literary" authors in everyday conversation. An entity called "literature" functions at the level of intersubjective and social relations; this much seems beyond question. Fine. But what have we proved? That in the broader system of a given society or culture, an identifiable element exists that is known by the label literature. Have we thereby demonstrated that all the particular products that take on the function of "literature" possess common characteristics, which we can identify with legitimacy? Not at all.

Question 46:
This passage casts doubt on :
items.explanation: The passage begins explicitly by stating: 'We need to begin by casting doubt on the legitimacy of the notion of literature', problematizing literature as a self-evident cultural category.

D. Periphrasis
List – II (Definition)
I. A unit of language that cannot be analysed into smaller units.
II. Refers back to a word or phrase previously used in a text/conversation.
III. Use of two or more words to express a meaning which could otherwise be expressed in a single word.
IV. A word or phrase that is referred back to by a pronoun or other proform.

items.title: Mock #07 · Q91
items.stem:
Read the passage and answer the questions given below:

Studies serve for delight, for ornament and for ability. Their chief use for delight is in privateness and retiring; for ornament, is in discourse; and for ability, is in the judgement and disposition of business. For expert man can execute, and perhaps judge of particulars, one by one; but the general counsels, and the plots and marshalling of affairs, come best from those that are learned. To spend too much time in studies is sloth; to use them too much for ornament, is affectation; to make judgement wholly by their rules, is the humour of a scholar. They perfect nature, and are perfected by experience: for natural abilities are like natural plants, that need pruning, by study; and studies themselves do give about them, won by observation. Read not to contradict and confute; not to believe and take for granted; not to find talk and discourse; but to weigh and consider. Some books are to be tasted, others to be swallowed, and some few to be chewed and digested; that is, some books are to be read only in parts; others to be read, but not curiously; and some few to be read wholly, and with diligence and attention. Some books also may be read by deputy, and extracts made of them by others; but that would be only in less important arguments, and the meaner sort of books, else distilled books are like common distilled water, fleshy things. Reading maketh a full man; conference a ready man; and writing an exact man. And therefore, if a man writes little, he had need have a great memory; if he confers little, he had need have a present wit: and if he reads little, he had need have much cunning, to seem to know that he doth not. Histories make men wise; poets witty; the mathematics subtle; natural philosophy deep; moral grave; logic and rhetoric able to contend.

Why should a man read books?
items.explanation: In 'Of Studies,' Francis Bacon advises that a person should read neither to dispute nor to passively accept ideas, but rather 'to weigh and consider' what is written in order to evaluate thoughts judiciously.

Some books are to be tasted, others to be swallowed, and some few to be chewed and digested; that is, some books are to be read only in parts; others to be read, but not curiously; and some few to be read wholly, and with diligence and attention. Some books also may be read by deputy, and extracts made of them by others; but that would be only in less important arguments, and the meaner sort of books, else distilled books are like common distilled water, fleshy things. Reading maketh a full man; conference a ready man; and writing an exact man. And therefore, if a man writes little, he had need have a great memory; if he confers little, he had need have a present wit: and if he reads little, he had need have much cunning, to seem to know that he doth not. Histories make men wise; poets witty; the mathematics subtle; natural philosophy deep; moral grave; logic and rhetoric able to contend.

How many categories the author has suggested for the purpose of reading?
items.explanation: Francis Bacon outlines three fundamental purposes for reading and study in his opening sentence: 'Studies serve for delight, for ornament and for ability.' These three categories represent private recreation, conversational eloquence, and practical execution in business.

items.title: Mock #07 · Q96
items.meta: Unit IV / Unit VIII: Prose & Criticism
items.stem:
Read the following stanza and answer the questions that follow:

When she rises in the morning
I linger to watch her
She spreads the bath cloth underneath the window
And the sunbeams catch her
Glistening white on the shoulders,
While down her sides the mellow
Golden shadow glows as
She stoops to the sponge, and her swung breasts
Sway like full-blown yellow
Gloire de Dijon roses.
She drips herself with water, and her shoulders
Glisten as silver, they crumble up
Like wet and falling roses, and I listen
For the sluicing of their rain-dishevelled petals.
In the window full of sunlight
Concentrates her golden shadow
Fold on fold, until it glows as
Mellow as the glory roses.

Which dominant rasa is there in the poem?
items.explanation: The poem evokes Shringara rasa (the aesthetic mood of romantic love and erotic beauty) through the intimate, sensual celebration of the woman's body, warm morning sunlight, and physical intimacy as she bathes.
